questiontext.text:
Goal

Write four one-line functions that divide, floor, take a remainder, and raise a number to a power.

How this works in Python

In Java the result of a division depends on the operands. Two int values give an int, and the fraction is thrown away before anything else happens.

int total   = 7;
int samples = 2;
int mean    = total / samples;   // 3, the .5 is gone
double real = 7 / 2;             // 3.0, because the damage was done first

That last line catches Java developers every year. The division ran as int arithmetic, and only then was the 3 widened to 3.0.

Python cannot make that mistake, because / never returns a whole number. Before the operators, meet the two numeric types.

  • int is a whole number, and it has no upper limit. A Java int wraps round to a negative value once it passes 2147483647, and a long runs out further along. A Python int grows to fit, so 2 ** 100 is an exact integer of 31 digits.
  • float is a number with a decimal point. It behaves exactly as a Java double does, because both follow the IEEE 754 standard. Python has nothing matching Java's 32-bit float, so the word float in Python means double in Java.

You never write either word in your code. Python reads the literal and picks the type. 3 is an int and 3.0 is a float.

Now the operators.

  • +, - and * behave as they do in Java. Two ints give an int, and one float anywhere in the sum gives a float.
  • / is true division. It always returns a float, even when the answer comes out whole. 6 / 3 is 2.0 and never 2. This is the single largest arithmetic difference between the two languages.
  • // is floor division. It drops the fraction and gives back an int when both sides are ints, so 17 // 5 is 3. This is the operator that does what Java's / does to two ints.
  • % is the remainder, as in Java. 17 % 5 is 2.
  • ** raises a number to a power, so 2 ** 10 is 1024. Java has no such operator and sends you to Math.pow, which hands back a double even when the answer is whole.

Keep every number in this question at zero or above. The two languages disagree about which way // and % round once a value goes negative, and that disagreement is the subject of the hard tier of this topic.

Your task

Write four functions. Each one is a single line.

  • mean_reading(total, samples) returns the average of total spread over samples. It returns a float every time, including when the division comes out whole.
  • full_crates(items, per_crate) returns how many whole crates the items fill.
  • loose_items(items, per_crate) returns how many items are left over.
  • cube(side) returns the side raised to the power of three.

You pass when the printed output matches the expected text exactly.

Rules
  • Do not call int(), float() or round() anywhere. The operator decides the type for you.
  • Do not write a type before a name, and do not write one after a name either.
  • Write no import line. Every operator here is built into the language.
  • Build the cube with **. Do not multiply the side by itself, and do not reach for a library.
Before you click Check

Write down what you expect each test to print. Then run it. A surprise means your model of Python is wrong, and that is the part worth learning.

AI protocol

No AI. Type every character yourself. This tier builds the muscle, and a tool that types it for you skips the exercise.

testcode.text: for items in (0, 5, 12, 100): print(items, mean_reading(items, 8), full_crates(items, 8), loose_items(items, 8)) print(mean_reading(10, 5) == 2, mean_reading(10, 5) == 2.0) print(cube(10) ** 2)

import ast, inspect for fn in (mean_reading, full_crates, loose_items, cube): tree = ast.parse(inspect.getsource(fn)) names = {n.func.id for n in ast.walk(tree) if isinstance(n, ast.Call) and isinstance(n.func, ast.Name)} assert not (names & {"int", "float", "round"}), "rule broken: no int, float or round conversions" assert not [n for n in ast.walk(tree) if isinstance(n, (ast.Import, ast.ImportFrom))], "rule broken: no imports" cube_tree = ast.parse(inspect.getsource(cube)) assert any(isinstance(n, ast.Pow) for n in ast.walk(cube_tree)), "rule broken: build the cube with the ** operator" print(mean_reading(1, 3)) print(full_crates(7, 7), loose_items(7, 7), cube(0))

questiontext.text:
Goal

Write four functions for a paint shop that round values up, down, to the nearest whole number, and to two places.

How this works in Python

Java's Math.round breaks a tie by going up. Math.round(0.5) is 1, Math.round(1.5) is 2, and Math.round(2.5) is 3. Round a long column of prices that way and the total creeps upwards, because every tie leans in the same direction.

long units   = Math.round(2.5);             // 3
double floor = Math.floor(7.9);             // 7.0, still a double
long tins    = (long) Math.ceil(45 / 12.0); // 4, and only after a cast

Python breaks a tie toward the even number instead. The rule is called banker's rounding, or round half to even. round(0.5) is 0, round(1.5) is 2, round(2.5) is 2, and round(3.5) is 4. Half the ties go up and half go down, so a long column does not drift.

round has two shapes, and they return different types.

  • round(x) with one argument returns an int.
  • round(x, n) with a digit count returns a float, rounded to n places after the point.

The second shape carries a trap that no rule about ties explains. round(2.675, 2) is 2.67 and not 2.68. The literal 2.675 has no exact binary form, so the value actually stored sits a shade below the tie, and Python rounds the number it holds rather than the number you typed. Java's Math.round(2.675 * 100) / 100.0 gives 2.68 because the multiplication lands on the other side of the line. Neither language is wrong about arithmetic. Both answers are facts about binary floats.

The rest of the work lives in a module. import math loads the module called math. A module is a file of ready-made code, and it is the closest thing Python has to a Java class full of static helpers. After the import, write math.ceil(...) with a dot, the way you write Math.ceil(...) in Java.

  • math.ceil(x) rounds up to a whole number and returns an int. Java's Math.ceil returns a double and leaves you to cast it.
  • math.floor(x) rounds down and also returns an int.
  • math.sqrt(x) returns a float, so math.sqrt(16) is 4.0.

Keep every value in this question at zero or above. Negative numbers change the direction math.floor travels, and that argument belongs to the hard tier of this topic.

Your task

Write four functions for a paint shop.

  • tins_needed(area, coverage) returns how many tins cover the area. Part of a tin is not for sale, so any remainder costs a whole tin. The answer is an int.
  • whole_metres(length) returns the length with the fraction dropped, as an int.
  • rounded_units(value) returns the value rounded to the nearest whole number, as an int. Predict all four tie cases before you run them.
  • line_total(unit_price, quantity) returns the price times the quantity, rounded to two places. The answer is a float, so a total that prints as 8.0 is correct and not a defect.

You pass when the printed output matches the expected text exactly.

Rules
  • Round with round and with math. Do not call int() to chop a decimal off.
  • Do not nudge a value with a small addition before rounding to force Java's answer out of it.
  • Write no if inside these four functions. A branch means you are fighting the rounding rule rather than using it.
  • import math is the only import permitted.
Before you click Check

Write down what you expect each test to print. Then run it. A surprise means your model of Python is wrong, and that is the part worth learning.

AI protocol

AI for explanation only. Ask it what an error means or why one form is more idiomatic. Do not let it write your answer.

testcode.text: print(rounded_units(0.5)) print(rounded_units(1.5)) print(rounded_units(2.5)) print(rounded_units(3.5)) print(line_total(2.675, 1)) print(line_total(19.99, 3))

import ast, inspect for fn in (tins_needed, whole_metres, rounded_units, line_total): tree = ast.parse(inspect.getsource(fn)) names = {n.func.id for n in ast.walk(tree) if isinstance(n, ast.Call) and isinstance(n.func, ast.Name)} assert "int" not in names, "rule broken: no int() to chop a decimal off" assert not [n for n in ast.walk(tree) if isinstance(n, (ast.If, ast.IfExp))], "rule broken: no if inside these functions" assert isinstance(tins_needed(5, 2), int), "tins_needed must return an int" assert isinstance(line_total(1.0, 1), float), "line_total must return a float" print(tins_needed(37, 12), whole_metres(99.999), rounded_units(4.5), line_total(0.125, 1))

questiontext.text:
Goal

Write five functions that split a shift and report how Python's division, rounding, and floats differ from Java's.

How this works in Python

In Java, 7 / 2 is 3 and -7 / 2 is -3. Both results truncate toward zero. Java's % then takes the sign of the left operand, so -7 % 2 is -1.

int shifts = total / workers;   // -7 / 2 gives -3
int left   = total % workers;   // -7 % 2 gives -1

Python splits those two jobs across two different operators and rounds the other way.

  • / is true division and always returns a float. 7 / 2 is 3.5, and 6 / 3 is 2.0 rather than 2.
  • // is floor division. It rounds down toward negative infinity instead of toward zero, so -7 // 2 is -4 and not -3.
  • % takes the sign of the right operand, so -7 % 2 is 1 and not -1.
  • ** raises a number to a power, so 2 ** 10 is 1024. Java has no such operator and sends you to Math.pow.

The two operators still agree with each other. For any a and any non-zero b, the expression (a // b) * b + (a % b) gives back a. Java holds the same identity under its own rounding rule. Neither language is broken. The two languages round in opposite directions, and the Python answer is the one you will not expect.

Python integers have no upper limit. A Java int wraps round to a negative number once it passes 2147483647. An overflow guard you would write in Java has nothing to catch here. 2 ** 100 is an exact integer of 31 digits.

round disagrees with Java as well. Java's Math.round always breaks a .5 tie upwards. Python uses banker's rounding, which breaks the tie toward the even number. round(0.5) is 0, round(1.5) is 2, and round(2.5) is 2. Across a long run of values, that rule does not drift upwards the way Java's rule does.

Floats behave exactly as a Java double does, because both follow the IEEE 754 standard. 0.1 + 0.2 is not 0.3 in either language. Python's standard library carries the repair. math.isclose(a, b) returns True when two floats sit near enough to each other to count as equal.

To reach that function you need one new statement. import math loads the module called math. A module is a file of ready-made code, and it is the closest thing Python has to a Java class full of static helpers. After the import, write math.isclose(...) with a dot, the way you write Math.abs(...) in Java.

Your task

Write five functions.

  • split_shift(total, workers) returns two values, the number of full shifts and the number left over, in that order. Write return full, leftover with a comma between the two names. The comma packs them into a tuple, which is a fixed group of values held in one object. One return then hands both back, and Python prints a tuple inside parentheses, as (3, 1). Java needs an array or a small class to carry a pair like that. Your answer must be right when total is negative, which is where a Java habit gives the wrong number.
  • division_report(), rounding_report() and float_report() each print the lines shown below. None of the three returns a value.
  • big_power() returns 2 ** 100.

Copy these lines exactly. The grader compares them character for character, spaces included.

7 / 2       = 3.5
7 // 2      = 3
-7 // 2     = -4   Java gives -3
-7 % 2      = 1    Java gives -1
int(-7 / 2) = -3   Java truncation
round(0.5) = 0   Java Math.round gives 1
round(1.5) = 2   Java Math.round gives 2
round(2.5) = 2   Java Math.round gives 3
0.1 + 0.2      = 0.30000000000000004
== 0.3         = False
math.isclose   = True

An f-string from the f-strings topic builds each of those lines. The float line needs the format spec {0.1 + 0.2:.17f}, which writes the sum with seventeen digits after the decimal point. Seventeen places is where the error becomes visible.

You pass when the printed output matches the expected text exactly.

Rules
  • Compare two floats with == exactly once, on the line that proves it is broken. Use math.isclose everywhere else.
  • Do not call int(), round() or abs() inside split_shift to patch up the negative case. The operators already floor correctly.
  • Write no if inside split_shift. If you needed a branch, you reached for the wrong operator.
  • Reach for int() only on the line that deliberately reproduces Java truncation, and label that line as such.
  • import math is the only import permitted.
Before you click Check

Write down what you expect each test to print. Then run it. A surprise means your model of Python is wrong, and that is the part worth learning.

AI protocol

AI allowed, on three conditions. Write your plan before you open it. Read every suggestion and reject the ones you did not plan. Type accepted code out yourself rather than pressing Tab.

expected.text: 7 / 2 = 3.5 7 // 2 = 3 -7 // 2 = -4 Java gives -3 -7 % 2 = 1 Java gives -1 int(-7 / 2) = -3 Java truncation round(0.5) = 0 Java Math.round gives 1 round(1.5) = 2 Java Math.round gives 2 round(2.5) = 2 Java Math.round gives 3 0.1 + 0.2 = 0.30000000000000004 == 0.3 = False math.isclose = True 1267650600228229401496703205376
-9 -> -3 shifts, 3 left, rebuilt -9 -1 -> -1 shifts, 3 left, rebuilt -1 0 -> 0 shifts, 0 left, rebuilt 0 1 -> 0 shifts, 1 left, rebuilt 1 9 -> 2 shifts, 1 left, rebuilt 9

testcode.text: import ast, inspect tree = ast.parse(inspect.getsource(split_shift)) assert not [n for n in ast.walk(tree) if isinstance(n, (ast.If, ast.IfExp))], "rule broken: no if inside split_shift" names = {n.func.id for n in ast.walk(tree) if isinstance(n, ast.Call) and isinstance(n.func, ast.Name)} assert not (names & {"int", "round", "abs"}), "rule broken: no int, round or abs inside split_shift" assert sum(isinstance(n, ast.Return) for n in ast.walk(tree)) == 1, "rule broken: one return statement" print(split_shift(0, 3), split_shift(-100, 7), split_shift(100, -7))
